chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ibn Mahboub, from Abu Ayoub, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said:
The one who brandishes the weapon in a city from the cities, so he injures, he would be retaliated due to it, and he would be exiled from that city.

And the one who brandishes the weapon in another city and strikes and injures, and takes the property, and does not kill, so he is a combatant, and his recompense is the Recompense of the combatant, and his matter is up to the Imam, if he so desire to he kills him, and if he so desires to, he crucifies him, and if he so desires to, he cuts his hand and his leg.

He said: And if he strikes and kills, and takes the property, so it is upon the Imam that he cuts his right hand due to the theft, then hands him over to the guardians of the murdered one, to pursue him for the property, then they kill him.

He (the narrator) said, So Abu Ubeyda said, May I be sacrificed for you! What is your view if he is forgiven by the guardians of the murdered one? So Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) said: If they excuse him from it, so it is up to the Imam that he kills him, because he has waged war, and killed, and stolen.

He (the narrator) said, So Abu Ubeyda said, What is your view if the guardians of the murdered one intend that the wergild (blood money) should be taken from it, and then leave him, is that for them (to do)? So he said: No. Upon him is the killing.
ai.seo_question: What is the difference in punishment for a combatant who injures versus one who kills and steals according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi elaborates on the jurisprudence of *al-Muharib* (the combatant), distinguishing between lesser aggression in urban centers and severe banditry involving killing and theft. It highlights the Imam’s discretionary authority (*ikhtiyar*) in applying the four penalties of Surah Al-Ma'idah, while establishing that the core act of waging war (*harb*) against the community makes the death penalty obligatory even if heirs forgive or accept blood money. This ruling underscores the public interest (*maslaha*) in maintaining security, prioritizing the state's right to execute over private compensation in cases of combined homicide and theft.
